nameStory: The Eared Grebe gets its name from the distinctive golden-orange feather tufts that sweep back behind its eyes during breeding season, looking remarkably like fancy ear ornaments. These 'ears' aren't really ears at all, but rather specialized feathers called auricular plumes that help the bird attract mates. It's also called the Black-necked Grebe in some parts of the world, referring to its striking dark breeding plumage.
description: The Eared Grebe is a compact, diving waterbird about the size of a small duck, with a pointed bill and distinctive lobed toes instead of webbed feet. During breeding season, it sports a jet-black head and neck contrasting sharply with bright golden-orange ear tufts and rusty-red flanks. In winter, it transforms into a more subdued bird with dark gray upperparts and clean white underparts. Like all grebes, it sits low in the water and is an excellent swimmer and diver.

idTips.label: Golden ear tufts (breeding)
idTips.description: Unmistakable wispy golden-orange feathers sweep back from behind the eye like streaming ribbons, creating an almost punk-rock appearance against the black head

idTips.label: Pointed, thin bill
idTips.description: Needle-like black bill is noticeably thinner and more pointed than a duck's bill, perfect for nabbing insects and small fish

idTips.label: Low water profile
idTips.description: Sits very low in the water with just the head, neck, and a bit of back visible, looking almost submarine-like as it glides along

idTips.label: Rusty-red flanks (breeding)
idTips.description: Rich chestnut-colored sides contrast beautifully with the white belly, like wearing a rust-colored vest

idTips.label: Lobed toes
idTips.description: If you're lucky enough to see one on shore, notice the bizarre toes with individual lobes rather than webbing - they feel rubbery and look almost alien

idTips.label: Gray and white (winter)
idTips.description: Winter birds lose all the fancy colors, becoming crisp gray above and bright white below with a clean dividing line

habitat: In New England, Eared Grebes are primarily found on larger freshwater lakes, reservoirs, and ponds, especially during migration periods. They prefer open water areas with little vegetation where they can dive freely for food. Occasionally spotted on coastal waters and salt ponds, particularly during fall migration when they may stop at places like Cape Cod's kettle ponds.

seasonality.spring: Rare spring migrants may show developing breeding plumage with partial ear tufts and darkening heads as they pass through in April and May.
seasonality.summer: Very uncommon in summer, with only occasional sightings of birds in full breeding plumage with golden ear tufts and black necks.
seasonality.fall: Peak viewing time from September through November when migrants appear in transitional plumage, gradually molting from breeding colors to winter gray-and-white.
seasonality.winter: Winter visitors are in plain gray and white plumage, looking quite different from their fancy breeding appearance, sometimes lingering on open water through December.

funFact: Eared Grebes can travel up to 3,700 miles during migration despite being such reluctant fliers that they prefer to dive underwater and swim away rather than take flight when threatened - making their epic journeys all the more impressive!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Horned Grebe, but remember 'Ears are higher' - Eared Grebes have golden tufts that sweep up and back from above the eye, while Horned Grebes have yellow tufts that stick straight out from behind the eye like horns. In winter, Eared Grebes have a cleaner white neck without the smudgy gray that Horned Grebes show.
contextualKnowledge: With only 53 recorded observations in New England, the Eared Grebe is considered quite rare in our region - most of the world's population migrates through western North America. Any sighting here is noteworthy and worth reporting to local birding communities or eBird, as these eastern appearances help scientists understand the species' range and migration patterns.
compareHints: Compared to its closest New England relatives, Eared Grebes are smaller than Red-necked Grebes (which have rusty necks in breeding plumage) and distinguished from Horned Grebes by their upswept golden ear tufts versus the Horned Grebe's straight-out yellow 'horns.' The Eared Grebe also has a slightly more upturned bill and cleaner white winter plumage than the Horned Grebe's somewhat dingy appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Horned Grebes are much smaller and more compact than Red-necked Grebes, which have longer, more snake-like necks and larger bills.
Red-necked Grebes are significantly larger than their closest New England relatives, the Horned and Eared Grebes.
